name: dynamic-proxy
intent: Generate the proxy class at runtime from the interfaces the caller names, instead of writing one forwarding class per subject, so that a single interception handler can extend every method of those interfaces.
problem: A hand-written proxy duplicates forwarding code per subject, per interface and per method: every method added to the subject means editing every proxy, and when the caller only learns the interface set at runtime (plugin hosts, containers, remote stubs, test frameworks) there is no class to write at all.
context: Applies wherever the platform can define a type at runtime (reflection, bytecode generation, trap-based proxy objects) and the subject's contract is expressed as interfaces or as overridable virtual members. Typical hosts are dependency-injection containers, object-relational mappers, remoting/API clients, test frameworks and language-interop layers; the pattern is usually infrastructure supplied by a framework rather than application code.
benefits: One interception class replaces a forwarding class per subject: a cross-cutting concern costs a handler, not N methods times M interfaces of boilerplate.
The proxied interface set can be decided at runtime, so containers, remoting stubs and test frameworks can proxy types they never saw at compile time.
Uniformity: every call passes the same funnel, so policy (transactions, retries, tracing, access checks) cannot be bypassed by a method somebody forgot to wrap.
Clients and targets stay untouched: callers keep programming against the interface, and the real subject remains unaware that it is proxied.
Late binding enables reversible and speculative behaviour - revocation, membranes, lazy loading, dirty tracking, spec-derived test doubles - that a compile-time wrapper cannot express.
tradeoffs: Every call pays for reflective dispatch: argument boxing, Method/MethodInfo invocation or trap dispatch, and megamorphic call sites that defeat inlining - visible in profiles of chatty interfaces.
Control flow becomes implicit and invisible in source: stack traces show generated frames, breakpoints land in generated code, and IDE navigation, find-usages and refactoring lose the call graph.

Type limits surface late: JDK/DispatchProxy proxies require interfaces, class proxies require non-final virtual members, and value, struct, enum or sealed types cannot be proxied at all, which pressures teams into extracting interfaces that exist only for the proxy.

Runtime code generation conflicts with AOT, trimming and native compilation (GraalVM native image, .NET NativeAOT with trimming, iOS/embedded) and is constrained by module systems and security policies, so the same design stops working when the deployment target changes.

Identity and lifetime get subtle: self-invocation inside the target bypasses the proxy, equals/hashCode/serialization and typeof/isinstance can disagree with the target, and generated classes plus long-lived handlers are a classloader/GC leak vector unless caches and references are bounded.

The encoding contract is unchecked: the handler must cover methods it never planned for - Object methods, interface default methods, void and primitive returns - and the compiler cannot prove that it does.

participants.responsibility: Calls methods through the interface it knows; it cannot tell whether the object it holds is the real subject or a proxy.
The type contract the proxy must implement, supplied at runtime; this is what makes generation possible without writing a class.

Type created at runtime that implements the subject interfaces and encodes each invocation as (method, arguments) for a single handler; it is cached per class loader or interface permutation, not per instance.
The one interception point: receives the encoded call, decides to forward, augment, short-circuit or synthesise a result, and owns the reference to the real subject.
The application object that performs the work; it is unaware of the proxy and of any behaviour added around it.

Runtime facility that defines or synthesises the proxy class and reuses an existing definition for the same interface set (JDK Proxy internals, DispatchProxyGenerator, the JavaScript Proxy constructor).

use_cases: Declarative cross-cutting concerns on service interfaces: transactions, retries, circuit breakers, metrics and tracing added by the container (Spring AOP with JDK proxies, .NET DispatchProxy or Castle DynamicProxy, Guice interceptors).
Remote and protocol stubs where the client declares only an interface: RMI, Retrofit-style API interfaces, gRPC/GraphQL clients, EJB and remoting proxies.
Persistence frameworks: lazy-loading stand-ins for expensive or not-yet-loaded entities, plus dirty-checking hooks for a unit of work (Hibernate and Entity Framework lazy proxies).
Test doubles derived from the real object at runtime (unittest.mock.create_autospec, Moq, NSubstitute, JMock), including verification of every interaction.
Capability membranes and revocable facades: mediating, filtering or revoking access to a sensitive target (Proxy.revocable in JavaScript, security wrappers around credentials or file handles).
Language-bridge objects for dynamic or scripted targets (Python/Swift interop proxies, @dynamicMemberLookup wrappers) and clients whose method set is discovered at runtime.

API client libraries with runtime discovery: Retrofit, GraphQL resolvers and gRPC-channel factories that receive a service interface and synthesise a network stub at first call rather than at compile time.
Access-control matrices where permissions are evaluated per call (ABAC/ACL middleware) — the proxy gates every operation without the service needing to know about the policy engine.
Distributed tracing and metrics: automatic instrumentation of any client that implements a traced interface, without modifying the client's source (OpenTelemetry gRPC/HTTP interceptors).
Database connection pooling and query timing: a proxy around java.sql.DataSource or a repository interface that records acquisition time, connection reuse counts and query latency per method.
Feature flags and A/B testing: a proxy that inspects a context and routes calls to one implementation or another, enabling traffic splitting without redeploying the service.
Schema-validation membranes: a proxy that validates outbound response payloads against a JSON Schema before serialisation, catching contract violations in integration tests rather than in production.

DI-container interception and typed factories generated by Castle DynamicProxy (Castle Windsor), and the .NET mocking engines layered on that same generator: Moq, NSubstitute, FakeItEasy, Rhino Mocks.

Annotated HTTP-interface stubs: Retrofit.create(service) validates the interface and returns a JDK dynamic proxy whose InvocationHandler turns each annotated method call into an HTTP request, caching one compiled ServiceMethod per method.
avoid_when: The proxy would wrap one known interface once: write the decorator or hand-written wrapper - it is type-checked, faster and readable.
The call sits in a hot loop or a tight latency budget: reflective dispatch and boxed arguments cost more than the concern they add; prefer a hand-written wrapper or generated code.

The subject is a value type, sealed or final class, struct, enum, or a Go/Rust/C interface with no runtime implementation: the platform cannot synthesise the subtype - use explicit forwarding or build-time generation.

The deployment forbids runtime code generation (NativeAOT with trimming, GraalVM native image, iOS, W^X-hardened sandboxes): generate the proxy at build time (source generator, annotation processor) or drop it.
A framework in the stack already proxies these components (Spring, Castle, Hibernate, the DI container): configure its interception instead of stacking a second proxy on top.
anti_patterns: Proxy by default: routing every service through a reflective proxy for one log statement, turning a straight call graph into an implicit one with generated frames in every trace.
Hidden behaviour: a handler that caches, retries, mutates arguments or swallows exceptions, so the call site no longer predicts what happens.
Fighting the type system: subclassing final classes, spoofing __class__ or monkey-patching to fake a proxy the runtime refuses to create.
One registry-sized handler holding every target and every generated class forever - a classloader/GC leak and a single point of contention.
Using the proxy to expose members the interface does not declare, forcing callers to cast or reflect, instead of extending the interface properly.
Treating the proxy as the object: identity comparisons, serialization and type checks that break as soon as the proxy replaces the target.
The proxy firewall: adding a proxy layer for every single method call just to log the method name, making every stack trace two frames deeper and making profiling output unreadable.
Surprise mutation: a handler that silently caches a return value, mutates an argument, or retries a call without documenting the behaviour, so callers cannot predict what happens.
One handler to rule them all: a single handler instance shared across all proxy instances with a switch statement routing to per-instance targets — a contention bottleneck and a maintenance hazard.
Finality violation: attempting to subclass a final class or override a final method via CGLIB/ByteBuddy, causing a runtime verification error or silent non-interception.

Module-boundary defiance: calling setAccessible(true) inside a module without --add-opens, catching the resulting InaccessibleObjectException and swallowing it instead of declaring the module dependency.

Proxy masquerading: returning a proxy where the caller expects the concrete type (e.g. passing a Hibernate proxy to a method that does instanceof checks on the real entity class), causing ClassCastException or false negative identity checks.
design_principles: Program to an interface: the proxy exists because clients depend on a contract instead of an implementation (JDK and DispatchProxy proxies cannot even be created without one).
Separation of concerns: interception policy lives in the handler, type plumbing in the runtime, and business logic in the target.
Open/closed principle: behaviour is added without modifying the target or its clients.
Composition over inheritance: forward to the target instead of subclassing behaviour into it; where subclassing is the only mechanism, virtual dispatch is the seam.
Liskov substitution and least surprise: the proxy must honour the subject's contract - same postconditions, honest identity, no invented return values.
best_practices: Generate the proxy type once per (class loader, interface set) and reuse it; put per-instance state in the handler, never in a shared handler.
Implement the handler as a small interceptor chain and make its thread-safety and state explicit; keep it free of hidden caches.
Decide and test how identity and default methods are handled (equals/hashCode/toString, __eq__/__hash__, ToString, interface defaults), then document the identity semantics the proxy exposes.
Handle self-invocation deliberately: return the proxy from accessors or use an explicit self-reference when internal calls must be intercepted.
Fail fast on an unhandled method - throw instead of returning null, undefined or zero - so missing handler branches surface in tests.
Bound the interception surface: proxy only the interfaces that need it, measure before putting reflective dispatch on a hot path, and move to build-time generation for AOT or trimmed deployments.
Close the ownership loop: release closures and revoke proxies when they are no longer needed, and make sure generated-type caches and handler registries cannot pin the target.

Treat the handler as an interceptor chain: separate each cross-cutting concern (retry, metrics, tracing) into a composable step so concerns can be added or removed independently without touching the core dispatch logic.

Make the handler stateless or clearly document its concurrency contract. Mutable shared handlers are a race-condition vector; prefer one handler instance per proxy instance or a thread-safe shared registry.

Define and test identity semantics explicitly — document whether equals/hashCode delegate to the target, whether a proxy equals its target, and whether a proxy of a proxy preserves the outermost identity. Inconsistent identity breaks collections, caches and assertions.
Use weak references for handler-to-target references when the target's lifetime is managed elsewhere, preventing the proxy from pinning the target and creating a classloader/GC leak.

On Java 9+: when calling setAccessible(true) inside a handler, open the required modules explicitly (--add-opens) rather than relying on a broad IllegalAccessException suppression; document the module requirements in the deployment descriptor.

For hot paths, benchmark reflective dispatch against a hand-written decorator; if the profiler shows visible overhead, generate the proxy at build time via an annotation processor or source generator instead of at runtime.

When the proxy must survive serialization (e.g. Hibernate, session replication), ensure the InvocationHandler/Interceptor and any hook/selector are themselves serializable, and test round-trip serialization in integration tests.
Instrument the proxy with a unique name or marker field so debugging and logging clearly distinguish proxy frames from real subject frames; avoid silent forwarding that obscures the call path.

Prefer interface-based proxies (JDK, DispatchProxy) over subclass-based proxies (CGLIB, ByteBuddy) unless you genuinely need to intercept protected or package-private methods; subclass proxies break when the subject class is sealed or final.

When stacking multiple proxies (proxy around proxy), collapse the chain at construction time rather than dispatching through N layers at every call; a single handler with an ordered interceptor list is faster and more debuggable.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Proxy: a surrogate controls access to a subject; the book already notes that the proxy class can be generated rather than written and that its interface set may be fixed at run time.
